analysis.one_liner: Makes losing Clean Water Act citizen-suit plaintiffs pay polluters' legal fees and strips the EPA's power to block wetland dumping sites.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its House subcommittee and expired at the end of the 116th Congress without a vote in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten three parts of the Clean Water Act. First, anyone who sues under the Act and does not win more than half of their claims would have to pay the other side's legal bills — a big financial risk for citizen groups that sue polluters. Second, it would repeal the EPA's authority to block dredge-and-fill dumping sites that would harm drinking water supplies, fisheries, wildlife, or recreation areas. Third, it would stop government agencies and court-approved settlements from requiring more wetland restoration than the existing regulatory minimum. The bill never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would have been land developers, homebuilders, and mining, energy, and agricultural operations that discharge dredged or fill material into wetlands and streams. They would face fewer citizen suits, could collect attorney fees from community groups that lose a case, and would no longer risk an EPA veto of a disposal site. Government agencies themselves also benefited from the provision limiting their own mitigation obligations.

how_it_helps.text: It converts Clean Water Act citizen-suit fee awards from a judge's discretionary call into a mandatory loser-pays rule, with the 'prevailing party' defined as whoever wins more than half the claims — exposing losing plaintiffs to the other side's attorney and expert fees.

It repeals Section 404(c) of the Clean Water Act, eliminating the EPA Administrator's power to deny or restrict a site for dumping dredged or fill material when the discharge would harm municipal water supplies, shellfish and fishery areas, wildlife, or recreation.

It bars federal courts from approving settlements — and bars government entities from agreeing — to wetland compensatory mitigation beyond the existing regulatory minimums, capping restoration obligations at the current rulebook.

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on people who depend on the Clean Water Act's protections: residents near proposed dumping sites, communities whose drinking water or shellfish beds could be affected, and conservation and citizen groups that could be forced to pay a polluter's legal fees for a partial win. Wetlands themselves — which absorb floods and filter water — would get less protection.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near polluting projects and citizen groups

drawbacks.text: The mandatory loser-pays rule is deliberately harsh: a citizen group that wins some claims but fewer than half of all claims in a case would have to pay the polluter's attorney and expert fees, which could discourage small organizations and individuals from filing Clean Water Act suits even when pollution is real.

Repealing Section 404(c) removes a backstop that has been used to stop disposal sites threatening municipal water supplies, shellfish beds, and wildlife areas even after the regular permitting process approved them — meaning questionable permits would have had no EPA override.

The prohibition on 'excess mitigation' would bar government entities from voluntarily restoring more wetland than regulations strictly require, even where local conditions called for it, and courts could no longer approve settlements in which an agency agrees to stronger mitigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have offered real relief from a genuine problem — a handful of costly, weakly-founded citizen suits can burden small landowners, local governments, and agencies — but it would have paid for that relief by cutting far more: it would have made polluters automatically able to collect fees from community groups that sue them, stripped the EPA of its authority to block disposal sites that threaten drinking water and fisheries, and barred agencies from restoring more wetland than the minimum rules require. On balance, the costs to water quality protections and to citizens' ability to enforce the Clean Water Act outweigh the benefit of deterring frivolous suits, and the bill's death preserved the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to a water subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled it for action, so it simply expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tom Rice introduced the bill on December 6, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

Three days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it stayed; the record shows no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action for the remaining thirteen months of the Congress.
The bill died with the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, having never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people and the communities that rely on the Clean Water Act kept its existing protections intact: the EPA's power to veto harmful dumping sites, citizens' right to sue polluters without risking mandatory fee awards, and current wetland mitigation standards all survived. Industry avoided neither a benefit nor a loss — the bill simply never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept existing wetlands protections

for.name: 30 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support on record; the bill never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would have shown how the parties split.

industries.note: Developers who fill wetlands face fewer citizen suits, an automatic fee shield if they win most claims in a case, and no EPA power to block a disposal site after permitting. Their cost savings come at the expense of the wetlands and waterways neighbors rely on.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and energy infrastructure
industries.note: Repealing Section 404(c) removes the EPA's authority to veto dredge-and-fill disposal sites for projects such as mines, pipelines, and terminals even where discharges would harm water supplies or fisheries — the last federal stop for the most damaging sites.

Mandatory loser-pays with a majority-of-claims threshold raises the financial risk of suing a polluter, since a group that prevails on some claims but fewer than half could owe the defendant's fees. Fewer suits mean less private enforcement of water pollution rules.

The bill caps compensatory mitigation at existing regulatory minimums and blocks courts from approving stricter mitigation in settlements, shrinking demand for mitigation projects — while easier permitting overall could still generate mitigation work.
